metadata.description: IoT / time-series event graph, FILE-BACKED over the wire: sustained ingest of time-stamped sensor readings under a sliding-window retention policy, driven over Bolt against a real graphus-server (real FileBlockDevice + real segmented WAL). Proves the durable on-disk store PLATEAUS under delete-old/insert-new churn while the server's reclamation counters climb — reclaimed space demonstrably reused, not unbounded growth.

notes: STORAGE RECLAMATION PLATEAU (the headline — FILE-BACKED, over the wire): over 140 ticks the workload ingested 7000 readings (35.0× the retention window of 200) into a REAL graphus-server (real FileBlockDevice + real segmented WAL) over bolt-uds. The durable data image PLATEAUED — post-warmup band [229376, 229376]B, ratio 1.000, page high-water 28 pages — while the server's own reclamation counters CLIMBED: graphus_maintenance_versions_reclaimed_total += 13600, graphus_maintenance_checkpoints_total += 45 over the same window (28 CHECKPOINT DATABASE statements issued). Both halves are needed: a flat store alone would also describe a workload that wrote nothing, and a climbing counter alone would not rule out unbounded growth.

DURABLE WRITE VOLUME (real, measured): the run wrote 142040524 WAL bytes CUMULATIVELY (the sum of the maximum length of every WAL segment ever seen — segments are append-only, and a checkpoint DELETES those below the reclaim floor, so the 1634347B of WAL still on disk at the end badly understates what was written). storage.bytes_fsynced carries that cumulative figure: every WAL byte is fsynced before its commit is acknowledged, so it is the honest durable-sync volume, not an fsync-syscall byte counter. write_amplification = (cumulative WAL + data image) / 189000 logical bytes ingested. The doublewrite buffer (8871936B) is a FIXED per-database preallocation and is deliberately NOT counted as store data — lumping it in would inflate the store and flatter every ratio. Independent cross-check from OUTSIDE the engine: the kernel accounted 189947904 write_bytes to the server process over the same window (/proc/<pid>/io).

FINDING — THE STORE PLATEAUS, AND SINCE rmp #706 THE DATABASE ON DISK VERY NEARLY DOES TOO. Read this next to the green `plateau_ratio: 1.000` above, which describes the STORE ALONE.
Measured on this run: the data image held FLAT at 229376 B across the whole post-warmup window, and the TOTAL durable footprint (store + WAL) now sawtooths within a TIGHT band [9369259, 14527355] B — a plateau ratio of 1.55 (down from ~7.1 while #706 was open), peaking at 63x per byte of graph (down from ~347x). The WAL is still most of the footprint, but it is now a small, bounded, sawtoothing multiple of the store rather than an unbounded climb to 64 MiB.
WHAT rmp #706 FIXED: WAL disk is reclaimed in whole SEGMENT units, and the active segment is never reclaimed — so nothing below the reclaim floor can be freed until a segment SEALS. The seal size is now STORE-PROPORTIONAL, clamp(store_bytes, 1 MiB, 64 MiB) (graphus_wal::segment_target_for_store), applied by the store at open and on every checkpoint. For a store this size that is the 1 MiB floor, so the reclaiming maintenance checkpoint — whose cadence #556 already made store-proportional — has small sealed segments below the floor to delete on nearly every pass. Before #706 the seal size was a fixed 64 MiB, so a small database's WAL climbed all the way to 64 MiB (hundreds of times its store) before one byte came back; a large log still keeps 64 MiB segments (the cap), unchanged.
WRITE AMPLIFICATION IS A SEPARATE, LARGELY-UNCHANGED NUMBER: the ~753x cumulative-WAL / logical-bytes figure is the record FORMAT (physiological redo + logical undo, dual imaging — rmp #556), NOT the reclaim granularity. #706 shrinks the RETAINED footprint on disk, not how many bytes each commit writes; reducing that would be a WAL-format change, out of scope here. So this figure barely moved (it was ~799x), and that is expected.
WHY THE RECLAMATION COUNTERS AGREE: graphus_maintenance_versions_reclaimed_total counts MVCC versions freed inside the STORE (what keeps the store flat); the on-disk WAL physically shrinking is the separate, direct proof that WAL disk came back. Both climb here.
OBSERVED THIS RUN: the run wrote 142040524 B of WAL, past the 67108864 B max-segment threshold, so it certainly sealed many (store-proportional) segments, and the on-disk WAL was seen to SHRINK 36 time(s), returning 96551056 B of disk — the WAL sawtooths in a tight band and comes back on nearly every checkpoint.
GUARDED: the file-backed regression guard in crates/graphus-cypher/tests/wal_amplification.rs now drives a REAL segmented FileLogSink and FAILS on a reverted (fixed-64-MiB) segment on a small store (rmp #719) — the MemLogSink guard it replaced had no segments and was structurally blind to this.

RECLAMATION IS OPERATOR-REACHABLE AND AUTOMATIC (rmp #305 — shipped; this example's earlier claim to the contrary was STALE and is corrected). Two real triggers exist in the live server: (1) `CHECKPOINT DATABASE <name>`, a parsed admin statement issued over Bolt/REST like any other — this run issued 28 of them over the wire; and (2) a background maintenance cadence that runs the same reader-safe GC + sharp checkpoint automatically once the WAL grows by clamp(4 × store_bytes, 8 MiB, 256 MiB) since the last pass, with no operator action at all. Set --checkpoint-every 0 to lean on the cadence alone.

CONCURRENCY: ingest ran over 2 concurrent Bolt connections, SHARDED BY SENSOR (a connection only ever writes readings from its own sensors), so no two writers contend for the same node's relationship chain — the realistic 'one gateway per group of devices' shape, and conflict-free by construction. Observed retries under SSI: 0 (abort_rate is that figure over all attempted statements — a real observation, not an assumption). The per-tick retention DELETE runs on the control connection AFTER the tick's ingest has fully drained, so it never races the writers.
